extracted.intended_audience: faculty members and academic researchers (early-career and experienced PIs) seeking grant funding
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for academics on how to respond to rejected grant applications: planning for rejection, obtaining and using reviewer feedback, deciding whether to reapply or seek alternate funders, and building psychological resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for rejection and build it into your schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The first key to dealing with rejection and negative feedback is to plan for it in advance and build it into your schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat applying as an iterative process: schedule time for reworking proposals after reviewer feedback. Especially for large, multidisciplinary team grants, plan to apply more than once rather than expecting a single attempt to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit to applying multiple times
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to commit to applying for it at least twice (if not three times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not permission to do a half‑hearted first submission; rather the strategy is apply, get feedback, and use that feedback to strengthen subsequent submissions. Repeated submissions are often necessary to become a funded PI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek negative feedback before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterintuitively, you may need to seek out negative feedback in advance of submitting a proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in outside readers or convene internal reviewers a few weeks before the deadline whose explicit role is to find all weaknesses so you can fix them before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional pre-review panels/readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a team within your university or bring together faculty and staff to pre-review key proposals (example: Eastern Michigan's Office of Research Development pre-review practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-review groups can boost campus success rates by identifying weak sections early. Schedule these reviews well before the deadline to allow time for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact program officer for reviewer comments and clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Once notice of rejection is received, contact the program officer for any copies of reviewer comments available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If comments are hard to decipher, a call to the program officer can help you get to the core of what reviewers found wanting. Use the officer to obtain the fullest possible feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically list and address every reviewer comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Look over the comments systematically, and list out areas where reviewers found weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a list of every single comment reviewers have made, and address each one in the next draft. Use this checklist to guide revisions and to demonstrate in resubmission how each concern was handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to reapply based on fit, scores, and comment tone
rubrics_metrics.description: If your comments are overwhelmingly negative, or sent back without comment, seriously rethink if this project should go back to the same agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor scores (e.g., only 50–60% of available points) or comments indicating a wrong turn may mean the idea is a poor fit for that funder or will not work; consider withdrawing and targeting a different program or funder instead of repeatedly reapplying to an unsuitable competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise the proposal by strengthening weak sections (evaluation, budget, institutional support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often reviewers point to items that were present in the RFP but in writing may have not gotten enough attention—sections such as evaluation, budget, institutional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix these weak sections, consult your grants office, experienced PIs, and academic leadership for concrete improvements, and ensure RFP requirements are fully and clearly addressed in the rewrite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and adjust team composition if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: You may need to bring in new members to your team or replace/drop members who seem to have dragged you down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer criticism can reflect weaknesses in personnel/roles. Reassess collaborators' contributions and credibility and restructure the team to strengthen the project in subsequent submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative funders or scale the project
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many ways to fund a project idea; sometimes you need more than just editing to make a project fundable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original funder is not a fit, adapt the proposal for different funders (e.g., use the structure to apply to a foundation for a more compact, fundable version). Repackaging or scaling can turn a rejected idea into a successful funded project elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept randomness; develop resilience and coping strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes fate deals you rejection without providing any useful information; a new review panel may not like the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop strategies to deal with the volume of rejection: view feedback as data rather than personal judgment, accept some outcomes as luck, and maintain persistence because not applying guarantees failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't let fear of rejection keep you from applying
rubrics_metrics.description: You are going to get 0 percent of the grants you do not apply for. Many faculty members fear rejection so much it keeps them out of the competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the career cost of non-submission; overcome perfectionism and fear by committing to the process of submitting and iterating, since many fundable ideas go unsubmitted due to fear.
